name: BitNet b1.58 (ternary LLM)
activation_scheme: activations remain 8-bit in the b1.58 recipe (weights are the ternary part); BitNet v2 explored sparsified lower-precision activations
kernels: llama.cpp and mlx community bitnet builds (unofficial)
quality_delta: From the paper, as a training result rather than a post-training delta: BitNet b1.58 'matches the full-precision (i.e., FP16 or BF16) Transformer LLM with the same model size and training tokens in terms of both perplexity and end-task performance', while being 'significantly more cost-effective in terms of latency, memory, throughput, and energy consumption' (quant-bitnet-paper). This is a matched-size-and-token-budget training claim, NOT an fp16-inference-baseline delta, and it is the paper's own headline rather than an independent replication.
notes: Every parameter is ternary {-1, 0, 1}. The framing that matters: this is a TRAINING-TIME recipe, not a post-training one. There is no such thing as PTQ-ing an existing fp16 LLM to 1.58 bits and keeping its quality - you constrain the weights to the ternary set during training. Read the quality claim correctly: 'matches fp16' means 'a ternary model trained from scratch on the same token budget matches an fp16 model trained from scratch on the same token budget', which is a statement about the expressiveness of the ternary set at fixed compute, not about quantization loss on a pretrained checkpoint. The paper explicitly frames 1-bit hardware as an open design target ('opens the door for designing specific hardware optimized for 1-bit LLMs'), so no accelerator here has a native ternary path. Confidence kept moderate because the authors label the paper 'Work in progress' and the match-claim is their own headline; no third-party perplexity comparison was located.
